pre: The investigation was undertaken to establish how the district of production, the length of post-harvest storage and the method of processing govern the quality of the traditional aromatic rice landraces of West Bengal, and to identify the cultivar and product combinations best suited to each end use. The findings of the three experiments are stated briefly below, and are drawn together in the overall summary and conclusion that follows.
E1: Three landraces, Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal and Kalojira, were grown at Nadia, Purba Bardhaman and Birbhum/Howrah and evaluated as fresh paddy and at 4, 8 and 12 months after harvest. Location, variety and storage each affected nearly every character determined. Birbhum and Howrah returned the best milling percentage, head rice recovery and bioactive fractions, Nadia the best hulling, soluble protein, fat, copper and zinc, and Purba Bardhaman the weakest values for most nutritional characters. Kalojira was the superior all-round landrace and Gobindabhog the better source of protein, iron and amino acids. Storage improved milling but reduced aroma by 31.7%, total phenol by 52.4% and antioxidant capacity by 62.7%, while the minerals held constant and phytic acid fell by 40.0%.
E2: Seven traditional products, four cooked and three processed, were prepared from nine aromatic cultivars together with the non-aromatic control Dudeshwar. The cultivars differed significantly for nearly every attribute in all seven products, whereas the year of production and its interaction with cultivar were significant for considerably fewer. On the composite quality score index the superior cultivar was Kalojira for table rice, Radhunipagal for khichdi, Kataribhog for pulao, Gobindabhog for payash and popped rice, Radhatilak for puffed rice and Harinakhuri for flattened rice, the control ranking at or near the bottom throughout. No single cultivar was superior for all seven products. Clustering placed the combinations in seven groups, five of them containing a single product only.
E3: Idli was prepared from the three aromatic landraces and the non-aromatic check, each plain and fortified with carrot or beet extract, giving twelve treatment combinations assessed on forty two parameters. Variety, fortification and their interaction were significant for most characters, fortification proving the stronger factor. The aromatic landraces exceeded the check for protein, phenol, flavonoid, antioxidant potential and every sensory attribute. Beet extract raised total phenol from 53.47 to 290.97 mg GAE 100 g⁻¹ and calcium from 61.44 to 550.88 mg L⁻¹, while carrot extract supplied β-carotene and gave the lowest predicted glycaemic index at 58.46. Overall acceptability was highest in KBI at 8.64 against 6.14 in the plain control product.
C1: The investigation establishes that the quality of the traditional aromatic rice of West Bengal is not a fixed property of the landrace. It is determined jointly by the genotype, the district in which the crop is raised, the period for which the paddy is held and the preparation for which the grain is finally used, so that any recommendation naming only the cultivar is incomplete. The three multivariate analyses of Experiment I concurred with the analysis of variance in ranking these influences: genotype was the strongest single determinant of grain quality, storage the next, and location the least influential overall, although decisive in particular instances of mineral composition, where a single landrace at a single site separated as a cluster of its own. The same ordering did not carry into the processed and cooked products, where the method of preparation fixed the broad quality type and the cultivar determined standing within that type, nor into the fermented product, where the type of fortification outweighed variety. The determinants of quality are therefore not fixed in rank across the value chain; they shift as the grain moves from field to store to kitchen, and a recommendation valid at one stage need not hold at the next.
C2: For grain quality the central finding is that storage acts in two opposing directions at once. Milling behaviour improves as the grain ages, head rice recovery gaining 2.13 percentage points up to eight months and amylose rising by 12.8% over the year, while aroma, soluble protein, lipid, phenol, flavonoid and antioxidant capacity all decline steeply over the same period, the last by 62.7%. These desirable attributes constitute a single tightly associated complex that falls in concert and cannot be recovered once lost, so the loss is not offset by the milling gain but merely accompanied by it. A holding period of four to eight months reconciles the two trends, since within that window the greater part of the milling gain has been secured while the loss of the health-promoting fractions remains moderate; where longer holding is unavoidable, cool storage merits consideration, since temperature rather than time governs the rate of these losses. Set against this, the four minerals remained unchanged while phytic acid declined by 40.0%, so that the phytate to mineral balance improves with ageing and aged grain should release its micronutrients more readily than fresh grain despite containing no greater quantity of them.
C3: For value addition the cultivar must be matched to the product, since no single entry proved superior across the seven preparations examined. Gobindabhog is indicated for payash and popped rice, Kalojira for table rice and for fermented idli, Radhunipagal for khichdi, Kataribhog for pulao, Radhatilak for puffed rice and Harinakhuri for flattened rice, and where a processor prepares more than one of these, Kalojira, Gobindabhog, Kalonunia and Radhatilak perform well across the widest range. In every product the aromatic landraces surpassed the non-aromatic control, so that substituting the cultivars named here would raise quality appreciably without any alteration in the method of preparation. In the fermented product, enrichment with beet or carrot extract improved the nutritional and sensory quality of idli without recourse to any synthetic colour or additive, beet-fortified Kalojira returning the highest phenol, flavonoid, antioxidant activity, soluble protein, anthocyanin and overall acceptability, and the carrot-fortified product the highest resistant starch with the lowest glycaemic response. The mineral gain from fortification is partly offset by an accompanying rise in phytate, so the phytate to mineral ratio rather than the mineral content alone should govern the nutritional claim.
C4: Three qualifications attach to these conclusions. The composite quality score index ranks the entries relative to one another and does not constitute an absolute scale, so it would require recomputation were further cultivars added; the trials covered two years and a limited number of sites, so confirmation over additional seasons and locations is required before any general recommendation is issued; and the amino acid profile was determined on freshly harvested grain alone, so no inference is drawn concerning the effect of storage upon it. Two observations lying far outside the remainder of the data, the length to breadth ratio of Radhunipagal at Purba Bardhaman at eight months and the near-absence of cysteine and tyrosine in Radhunipagal, should be verified against the raw records. Subject to these reservations, the practical implication is clear. The premium these landraces command rests upon the attributes most rapidly forfeited in store, so its realisation depends upon the marketing chain as much as upon the breeding programme, and a grower, miller or processor who fixes the landrace correctly but the storage period wrongly will forfeit much of what the crop was grown for.
C5: The wider significance of the work lies in the objective, location-specific quality data it provides for a group of landraces that has been valued hitherto on reputation and custom. Four of the cultivars examined, Gobindabhog, Tulaipanji, Kalonunia and Radhunipagal, carry Geographical Indication protection, and the district-wise values reported here furnish a basis for authentication, for the fixing of safe storage periods and for market development. The demonstration that these landraces yield superior processed, cooked and fermented products, and that a traditional fermented food may be enriched in phenolics, antioxidants, provitamin A and minerals using two commonly available vegetables alone, offers a practical route to adding value to indigenous germplasm rather than displacing it. Taken with the nutritional superiority of the aromatic landraces over the non-aromatic control across every experiment, the results furnish a scientific justification, additional to the cultural and aromatic value already recognised, for the continued cultivation and conservation of the traditional aromatic rice of West Bengal, and for its promotion as the basis of a value-added food industry rooted in the state.
